chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Haytham al-Ajali (may Allah have mercy on him) narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Zakariya al-Qattan narrated to us, saying: Bakr ibn Abdullah ibn Habib narrated to us, from Tamim ibn Buhlul, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Hammam ibn Hamran, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) say:

The one who takes his knowledge as a livelihood will become poor. So I said to him: May I be sacrificed for you, indeed, among your Shi'a and befrienders there are people who carry your sciences and spread them among your Shi'a, and they are not prevented from them, of goodness, connection and generosity. Then he, peace be upon him, said: Those are not ones who take it as a livelihood. The one who takes his knowledge as a livelihood is only the one who issues verdicts without knowledge nor guidance from Allah, Exalted and Glorious is He, with the purpose of invalidating rights out of greedy for the wracks of this world.

key_terms.اسْتَأْكَلَ: To take something as a livelihood or means of sustenance
key_terms.الصِّلَةَ: Connection, kinship ties, or continuous support
key_terms.حُطَامِ الدُّنْيَا: The wracks or fleeting gains of the worldly life
key_terms.عِلْم: Knowledge, specifically religious or scholarly knowledge
key_terms.يَفْتِي: To issue a religious verdict or fatwa

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between teaching knowledge for the community and taking knowledge as a livelihood in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In *Mani al-Akhbar*, Shaykh al-Saduq records Imam al-Sadiq’s distinction between legitimate scholars who disseminate knowledge for the community’s benefit and those who 'take knowledge as a livelihood' (*musta’kil*) by issuing fatwas primarily for worldly gain. The Imam clarifies that the true danger lies not in receiving support, but in using religious authority to invalidate rights (*hukoom*) through ignorance or bias, driven by the desire for *hutam al-dunya* (the fleeting allure of the world). This highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on sincerity (*ikhlas*) and the integrity of religious judgment over mere financial sustenance.
